title: Mona Lisa
summary: The Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait painting by the Italian artist Leonardo da Vinci. Considered an archetypal masterpiece of the Italian Renaissance, it has been described as "the best known, the most visited, the most written about, the most sung about, [and] the most parodied work of art in the world". The painting's novel qualities include the subject's enigmatic expression, the monumentality of the composition, the subtle modelling of forms, and the atmospheric illusionism.

sections.name: her face
sections.description: The face of Lisa Gherardini with her legendary enigmatic smile. Leonardo used sfumato to create soft, smoky transitions between light and shadow, giving her a lifelike quality.

sections.name: her hands
sections.description: Her hands are crossed gracefully in her lap, resting on the arm of a chair. This pose represents composure and modest virtue, common in high-society Renaissance portraits.

sections.name: the landscape
sections.description: The background shows a misty, imaginary landscape with a winding road on the left and a bridge on the right, leading into jagged blue mountains.

guide_notes.her face: Her face is a smooth oval dome rising above the cloth of her shoulders, and your fingers will find almost no hard edges anywhere on it — the brow, cheek and jaw melt into one another like a continuous slope instead of meeting at lines. Trace the centre: a straight nose widens gently, and beneath it the mouth is only a faint crease whose corners turn up so slightly that the smile seems to change depending on where your hand rests. The eyes sit level with the horizon behind her, their lids rounded and unoutlined, so the whole face reads as calm and unbroken under the fingertips. A multispectral scan in 2004 found a single faint eyebrow hair hidden beneath the paint — evidence that Leonardo did paint brows and lashes that were later lost, most likely wiped away by centuries of cleaning.
guide_notes.her hands: At the lower centre of the relief, two hands rest one on top of the other — the right laid softly across the left wrist — forming a rounded mound that anchors the whole composition. Your fingers will feel the left forearm entering from the left edge, then the right hand draping across it, its long fingers slightly curled and relaxed with the knuckles barely raised. The skin here is modelled as smoothly as her face, and the sleeves pile in soft, heavy folds around the wrists before spilling out of the frame. Leonardo deliberately omitted a wedding ring and used this crossed-hand gesture instead, reading it as a sign of a virtuous and faithful wife.
guide_notes.the landscape: Behind her shoulders the relief opens into deep space: on the left a low winding road curls back toward rocky ground, while on the right a river runs beneath a small arched bridge — your fingertips can trace the road as a raised thread and the bridge as a row of little bumps. Around these, the forms grow softer and paler the farther back they sit, with the near rocks standing out sharply while the distant peaks dissolve into a smooth, faint haze. Notice that the two sides never quite meet: the horizon on the left sits lower than the horizon on the right, so the landscape does not join up behind her head. That bridge was identified in 2023 by the historian Silvano Vincenti as the Romito di Laterina bridge in Tuscany, a real structure Leonardo would have known.

museum_facts: The Louvre identifies the sitter as Lisa Gherardini, wife of Florentine silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo; her name gives the painting its Italian title, La Gioconda.
Leonardo used sfumato, layering glazes to create soft, smoky contours. The sitter’s turn toward the viewer adds a sense of natural movement.
The painting is on a poplar-wood panel, not canvas. The panel has warped and developed a crack, so the Louvre displays it in a temperature- and humidity-controlled glass case.
King François I invited Leonardo to France and bought the painting from him in 1518, bringing it into the royal collection.
The painting was stolen from the Louvre on 21 August 1911 and recovered more than two years later after former Louvre glazier Vincenzo Peruggia tried to sell it to an Italian art dealer.
